newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX oil complex ends lower amid a consolidation.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX oil complex ends lower amid a consolidation.

text.p: The NYMEX oil complex ended lower Monday as prices fell into technical consolidation following a sharp run-up last week, traders and analysts said.
"I have been looking for crude to consolidate between $23.00 to $24.00 since last Tuesday," said Tim Evans of Pegasus Econometric Group.
October crude settled down 12 cents to $23.73 a barrel. Last Tuesday, the spot month hit a life-of-contract high of $24.25 on news that the Iraqi oil-for-food deal was suspended.
"If crude holds in the upper end of the ($23.00-$24.00) range, it suggests the uptrend will continue," Evans said.
Crude prices pulled back today after being unable to break resistance of $24.00.

Still, traders said crude will need technical strength to take it higher as little change in the status of the suspended Iraqi oil-for-food deal was expected this week since Kurdish factions continued fighting in northern Iraq.
Jim Ritterbusch, a trader with Sweeney Oil, said crude mostly followed gasoline lower due to lack of news.
October gasoline settled down 1.18 cents to 64.09 cents a gallon. October heating oil closed down 0.45 cent to 65.95 cents a gallon.
"Gasoline was pulling everything down today," said Ritterbusch.

Refined product prices received no upside support from Hurricane Hortense which was a weak Category 1 hurricane with 80 mile-per-hour winds. At 1400 EDT/1800 GMT, Hortense was 130 miles southeast of Ponce, Puerto Rico and moving northwest.
Hortense bypassed Amerada Hess Corp's huge refinery on St. Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands, while Sun Co was monitoring the hurricane in light of its 85,000 barrel-per-day refinery on Puerto Rico.
Several traders called a lower open for the NYMEX oil complex Tuesday ahead of weekly data on oil inventories by the American Petroleum Institute (API) Tuesday evening.

But, Ritterbusch said the API data could be bullish, and he estimated distillate stocks about unchanged with the week before at a time when there should be builds of around two to three million barrels in preparation for winter.
"There was some movement from primary to secondary stocks as prices went high," Ritterbusch said, explaining his reasoning for a lack of build in distillate stocks.
Though weaker at the close, heating oil prices remained tightly backwardated amid historically low inventories.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
